title: Pain assessment

sources.use: Open RN Nursing Fundamentals (CC BY): landing and TOC only
narrative review of pain evaluation in non-verbal critical care patients (CC BY)

objectives: Assess pain routinely with the unit's tool and reassess after interventions.
Treat pain before considering a sedative.

items.text: Assess pain routinely and before and after painful procedures.
Treat pain before considering a sedative (SCCM good-practice statement).

When the patient cannot communicate or show pain behaviours, do not infer absence of pain from the monitor or immobility. Assess likely painful conditions and procedures, verify the authorised analgesia plan and seek clinical review.

Document with the unit's tool and reassess after any intervention; use an assessment-driven, protocol-based, stepwise approach where the unit has one (SCCM suggestion, moderate certainty) and titrate only within the protocol.

The narrative review recommends structured training (including simulation-based practice and ongoing support) and standardised local protocols so a behavioural tool is scored consistently between staff, and recommends integrating the tool into the electronic record with regular audit and feedback to support consistent use.
Analgesic choice and dosing are prescriber or protocol decisions and are not given in this library.
For patients who cannot self-report, behavioural tools are used; item descriptors and thresholds are not reproduced here.

A commonly used behavioural tool (the Critical Care Pain Observation Tool) observes four domains - facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, and ventilator compliance (or vocalisation for a non-intubated patient) - without reproducing its scoring thresholds here; the narrative review reports its facial-expression item may be unreliable in patients with facial paralysis, neuromuscular disorders, or those receiving a neuromuscular blocker, and notes inter-rater reliability is acceptable but variable between scorers.

When the patient cannot self-report but observable behaviour is present, the SCCM PADIS statements support BPS, BPS-NI or CPOT for the appropriate ICU population. Use the unit's validated version and staff training; these are not interchangeable numeric scales. If behaviour is unobservable, record the limitation and seek a clinical pain-management plan.

Where possible, enable reliable patient self-report using an appropriate communication aid or visual scale. When reliable self-report is not possible, family observations may help identify usual expressions of discomfort, but do not replace a validated behavioral assessment when applicable. Changes in vital signs should trigger further assessment rather than be converted into a pain score.
SCCM suggests massage and music therapy may be offered (conditional, low certainty) and suggests not offering virtual reality or hypnosis (conditional, very low).
Reassess after every intervention and before and after painful procedures.
Report uncontrolled or escalating pain to the prescriber.

For new severe pain, clinical deterioration or suspected analgesic-related respiratory depression, obtain urgent clinical help; reassess breathing and arousability as well as pain after interventions.
Record tool, score, interventions and response per your unit's documentation standard.

checklist.text: Seek the patient's own pain report whenever possible. If self-report is not possible and pain behaviours are observable, use a validated behavioural tool according to local policy.
Assess before and after painful procedures.
Treat pain before considering a sedative, within the protocol.
Offer non-drug measures your policy allows.
Report uncontrolled pain to the prescriber.

If paralysis or another condition makes behaviour unobservable, record the assessment limitation; immobility does not establish comfort. Vital-sign changes are prompts for assessment, not a substitute pain score.

When the patient cannot self-report but observable behaviour is present, the SCCM PADIS statements support BPS, BPS-NI or CPOT for the appropriate ICU population. Use the unit's validated version and staff training; these are not interchangeable numeric scales. If behaviour is unobservable, record the limitation and seek a clinical pain-management plan.

Where possible, enable reliable patient self-report using an appropriate communication aid or visual scale. When reliable self-report is not possible, family observations may help identify usual expressions of discomfort, but do not replace a validated behavioral assessment when applicable. Changes in vital signs should trigger further assessment rather than be converted into a pain score.
